note: Synthetic data, fictional company. Written by scripts/assistant_examples.py.

answers.question: Which uncovered customers are most at risk of leaving right now, and why?
answers.answer:
The uncovered customers most at risk of leaving are small-business accounts. Uncovered customers are the ones with no assigned success manager. Eldenta Retail is the highest, with a modeled 76% chance of leaving in the next 90 days.

| Customer | ARR (annual recurring revenue) | Churn risk | Main reasons |
|---|---|---|---|
| Eldenta Retail | $1,764 | 76% | Many high-priority and other support tickets, setup incomplete |
| Kelomi Energy | $717 | 60% | Setup incomplete, never answered the NPS survey (NPS is a 0 to 10 satisfaction score), reads our emails |
| Drinolo Software | $1,411 | 45% | Setup incomplete, never answered NPS, admin rarely logs in |
| Norora Logistics | $1,771 | 42% | Few seats active, setup incomplete, never answered NPS |
| Iskuvia Logistics | $0 | 36% | Setup incomplete, never answered NPS, nearly all seats assigned |

Incomplete setup shows up for every customer in the top eight. Never answering the NPS survey shows up for most of them. Eldenta Retail is the only one with a support problem as a main reason. Of the 159 uncovered customers, 40 are flagged "High risk of leaving", and together they represent $61,832 in ARR.

Source: gold.account_current
sql: select account_name, segment, arr, round(churn_risk_score,2) risk, health_band, days_to_renewal, churn_top_reasons from gold.account_current where coverage_tier='uncovered' order by churn_risk_score desc limit 8
select count(*) n, sum(case when churn_risk_high then 1 else 0 end) high, sum(case when churn_risk_high then arr end) high_arr from gold.account_current where coverage_tier='uncovered'

answers.question: How much annual revenue do the customers in the pilot represent, and how much of it is in the red health band?
answers.answer:
The 159 customers in the pilot (those with no assigned success manager, called the "uncovered" coverage tier) represent $366,004 in annual recurring revenue (ARR). Of that, $14,590 is in the red health band, which is the lowest of the three bands (green, yellow and red). The red amount comes from 5 customers, or about 4% of the pilot's ARR. These figures are as of today, 2026-09-07.

Source: gold.account_current
sql: select count(*) n, sum(arr) total, sum(case when health_band='red' then arr end) red, sum(case when health_band='red' then 1 end) red_n from gold.account_current where coverage_tier='uncovered'

answers.question: Which play has the most customers in it right now?
answers.answer:
The Onboarding rescue play has the most customers in it right now, with 4 customers still in progress. Usage recovery and Reference request each have 2, and Seat expansion and Detractor save each have 1.

answers.question: How many customers were kept out of a play, and for what reasons?
answers.answer:
Two things could count as "kept out", so here are both.

**Held out on purpose (the holdout):** 47 enrollments were held out, covering 45 distinct customers. The holdout is a share of eligible customers who are deliberately left alone so the play's effect can be measured. The only reason is that they were chosen for comparison. Some customers were held out of more than one play, which is why 47 is larger than 45.

**Eligible but removed from a play after it started (exited):** 22 customers.

| Exit reason | Customers |
|---|---|
| A person tried and got no response | 16 |
| A person judged the customer not a fit | 6 |

I found no other recorded reason in the enrollment data. This table also doesn't record customers who were never eligible, for example because they have no contact we may email.

Source: silver.stg_ops_enrollments
sql: select arm, status, coalesce(exit_reason,'(none)') r, count(*) n, count(distinct account_id) a from silver.stg_ops_enrollments where arm='holdout' or status='exited' group by 1,2,3 order by n desc

answers.question: Which records were rejected when the data arrived, and why?
answers.answer:
In the current warehouse run, 1,318 of 100,326 product event lines were rejected at ingest and sent to the dead-letter queue. That is the holding area for rows that can't be used. The reasons are:

| Reason | Rows |
|---|---|
| No account id | 1,004 |
| Unknown event name | 268 |
| Broken JSON (the line can't be read) | 46 |

Rejected events are only those that can't be used at all. Other problems are loaded and repaired later in the pipeline instead of being rejected:
- 438 duplicate events removed.
- 185 future-dated events removed.
- 108 late-arriving events kept under their true date.
- 9 duplicate contacts removed.

A rejected event can hide a real fact. For example, a lost setup step can make an account look one step behind until the dead letter is replayed. Seat counts are not affected, because they come from the licence snapshot.

Source: gold.dq_summary, docs/decisions/0009-ingest-validation-and-dead-letter.md

answers.question: What are the five parts of the health score, and how much does each one weigh?
answers.answer:
The health score is a weighted sum of five parts. Each part is scored from 0 to 100.

| Part | Weight | What it measures |
|---|---|---|
| Adoption | 35% | Share of assigned seats active this month (60%) and setup completion (40%) |
| Sentiment | 20% | Latest survey score times 10, or 60 if the customer was never surveyed |
| Engagement | 15% | Email open rate (70%) and admin logins (30%) |
| Support | 15% | 100 minus penalties for open and recent high-priority tickets |
| Commercial | 15% | Seat utilization (50%) and whether seats are growing, flat or shrinking (50%) |

A score of 70 or above is green, 50 to 69 is yellow, and below 50 is red.

Source: docs/metrics.md

answers.question: How many conversations did the AI agent have, and why were some passed to a person?
answers.answer:
The AI agent had 7 conversations in total, and all 7 were passed to a person. None were marked as resolved by the agent.

| Reason for handoff | Who decided | Conversations |

answers.question: When must the AI agent hand a conversation to a person?
answers.answer:
The AI agent must hand a conversation to a person when any of these hard rules fires. They are enforced in code, so the model can't talk its way around them.

- **Customer asks for a person.** This goes to the Scaled CS team.
- **Customer is frustrated.** Either keywords or a classifier score of 0.7 or higher triggers it. This goes to the Scaled CS team.
- **Pricing or upgrade question.** This goes to Account owners (Sales).
- **Contract, refund, billing or legal question.** This goes to the Scaled CS team.
- **The help center doesn't cover the question.** The agent may ask one clarifying question first. Then it goes to the Scaled CS team.
- **A tool fails or times out.** The agent hands off and never guesses. This goes to the Scaled CS team.
- **The same question comes back a second time.** This goes to the Scaled CS team.
- **The model is unavailable, declines, or asks to hand off.** This goes to the Scaled CS team.

The first three rules run before the agent model is called at all, so a pricing question never reaches it. A handoff can also happen when a play's ladder reaches its human step. For example, in the Onboarding rescue play, a person steps in if the agent escalates or setup is still stalled 4 days after the agent step. Separately, the mailbox triage agent sends replies to a person when they contain a complaint, buying intent or a meeting request, or when the classifier is unsure.

Source: docs/human-fallback.md, docs/play-specs/onboarding_rescue.md

answers.question: Did the onboarding play work against its holdout?
answers.answer:
We can't tell yet. The Onboarding rescue play has too few customers to give a reliable result. The treated group has 10 customers and the holdout group has 12. A holdout is a share of eligible customers kept back so we can measure the play's effect. The result is flagged "too early" because it needs at least 20 customers in each group.

The setup completion rate was 20% for treated customers (2 of 10) and 8.3% for the holdout (1 of 12). That is a lift of about 11.7 percentage points. The 95% confidence interval runs from -17.6 to +41.0 points, and the p-value is 0.43. The interval includes zero, so this gap could easily be chance. The recommendation is to keep testing.

Source: gold.experiment_results
sql: SELECT * FROM gold.experiment_results WHERE play LIKE '%onboarding%'

answers.question: How is a holdout chosen, and why does it matter?
answers.answer:
A holdout is a group of qualifying customers who get no help from a play, so the play's effect can be measured against them. The system picks that group with a fixed formula (a hash) of the account, the play and the play's version. It doesn't use a random draw. That formula also decides whether the account falls inside the 10% rollout slice.

Because it's a formula, the same account always gets the same answer on any machine and on any day. Nobody can nudge an account into treatment, and re-running the engine never reshuffles the groups. Raising a play's version reshuffles them on purpose. Exclusions are applied before assignment, so they can't favor one group.

A holdout counts as a real enrollment that receives nothing. While the measurement window lasts, it also keeps the account out of other exclusive plays, so another play can't contaminate the comparison. The account is released afterward.

Pilot holdouts are large because a small holdout learns slowly:
- Most plays hold out 50%.
- The Detractor save play holds out 20%, because withholding help from an unhappy customer has a real cost.
- The Find the admin play holds out 0%, because it is data hygiene and not an experiment.
- Plays that scale after the pilot move to a 10% standing holdout.

This matters because the holdout is the only fair baseline. Without a comparable group that got nothing, you can't tell whether customers improved because of the play or would have improved anyway. The system also checks that the treatment and holdout split matches the design. In one case the Seat expansion play showed 91 treatment and 58 holdout accounts against a 50/50 design. That turned out to be chance, because the hash had assigned 93 and 60.

Source: docs/decisions/0014-plays-as-config-with-deterministic-holdouts.md and docs/decisions/0016-experiment-design-for-the-pilot.md
